extracted.intended_audience: Investigators applying for NIH grants (K, R, DP2, R01, R21, R34, etc.), including early-career and established biomedical researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, experience-based guidance on preparing, submitting, and navigating NIH grant applications (study section choice, PO interactions, paylines, JIT/admin review, clinical trial requirements, resubmission strategy, and timelines). Aimed at maximizing funding chances and handling post-review steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult a Program Officer early
rubrics_metrics.description: Find and talk with a PO who is excited about your work; the PO can provide guidance on how to frame your research (basic advice, not actual help with the narrative). If you have not found such a PO, then you might want to start there. If you have a helpful PO, great. If not, Matchmaker is another option to help find one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contacting a PO early can prevent spending effort on science that isn't a high priority for the IC. POs can advise on study section choice and whether to pursue select pay or co-funding. Use NIH Matchmaker to locate an appropriate PO if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match your application to the right study section
rubrics_metrics.description: When you narrow down your choice, search RePORTER for currently funded projects that were reviewed in that study section. Some might be select pay awards, but you can assume the list of awards coming back represents the type of work that got the reviewers excited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your project doesn’t look anything like those, consider other study sections or ICs. Study section composition matters (e.g., engineering reviewers vs. clinical reviewers) and can hugely affect whether reviewers are excited by your proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use RePORTER to infer reviewer priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Search RePORTER for projects reviewed in a study section to see the types of work that excited reviewers and were funded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the returned awards list as representative examples of successful science for that study section; use it to assess fit and decide whether to pursue that study section or try another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and check IC-specific paylines and practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Paylines vary by IC (e.g., 'NINDS payline 14% in 2021', 'NIAID K payline 20 for some Ks but K99 may differ'), and ICs differ in whether they give New Investigator breaks or recognize ESI status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask your PO about current payline expectations and whether New Investigator or ESI status affects funding. Don’t assume uniform rules across ICs; some ICs do select pay, some do not publish paylines, and some give weight to ESI/NI status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask your PO about select pay and co-funding possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Select pay (promoting an application just over the payline) and co-funding (e.g., IDeA co-funding) depend on PO enthusiasm and institutional procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PO needs to initiate both promotion for select pay and nominations for co-funding; secondary ICs almost never fund unless strongly interested. Timing of these actions and whether they will be pursued is best confirmed with the PO after summary statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret 'Pending' and 'Pending Administrative Review' statuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Status changes to 'Pending' or 'Pending Administrative Review' after Council usually indicate the application is under consideration for funding at some administrative level (often pre-award/JIT stage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'No difference – something is happening with your application (possibly waiting for the JIT review, possibly waiting for something else).' If you haven't been asked for JIT, you may get a request soon; if you already submitted JIT, they may be reviewing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: JIT (Just-In-Time) requests signal administrative interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Receiving a JIT request or personalized JIT from Grants Management Specialist is a positive sign that your application is being moved toward award consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all applications receive JIT; timing varies. Respond promptly and accurately to JIT requests (e.g., clinical trial milestones, Other Support) when asked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other Support requests are a good sign
rubrics_metrics.description: Being asked to send Other Support for Key Personnel often means the IC is looking at the application for a possible award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not a guarantee, such requests typically indicate administrative attention; follow up with PO if uncertain about implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: IACUC/IRB approvals affect timing but not usually funding decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: An expired IACUC protocol discovered during JIT/administrative review may delay the award but typically will not change the decision to fund.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If renewal will take time, inform the Grants Management Specialist with an estimated approval date. The IC may issue the award but hold funding for animal purchases until approvals are in place.

rubrics_metrics.name: R56/bridge awards are discretionary and depend on PO judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: R56 decisions are up to the PO and are influenced by availability of funds, whether the lab would shut down without funding, and whether the research is a high priority for the IC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may not hear about R56s until late in the fiscal cycle; apply again and improve score while awaiting possible bridge funding decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical trial applications: IND and mechanism considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: If a trial seeks FDA approval you generally need an IND; NIH will fund therapies developed by private companies, but NIH is 'very very picky about the trials they fund.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Talk to a PO before planning a trial. For multisite clinical trials, many ICs now require an R34 planning award before they will accept an R01 with a clinical trial; for pilot data look at R21 FOAs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competing revision vs renewal (structural differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: A competing revision requests expanded scope/additional funds to an active award (can only be submitted while award active with ≥1 year remaining). A renewal requests continued support (submitted later, typically in year 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They are different mechanisms and you wouldn't choose between them without regard to award timing and intent; discuss with your PO which is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: K award effort requirements and reductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ks generally require substantial effort (often at least 75%); reductions in effort are typically allowed in later years to permit transition to independent R01 funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effort reductions are handled during JIT/administrative review, not in advance. Talk with PO for specifics (some K variants differ).

rubrics_metrics.name: When near but outside a payline, consider resubmission
rubrics_metrics.description: If your score is just outside an IC payline (e.g., 15% when payline is 14%), resubmission may be advisable rather than waiting for select pay decisions that may occur late or not at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss with PO about likelihood of select pay; don’t risk losing a cycle if you are close. Prepare A1/resubmission strategically using summary statement feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect long, sometimes unpredictable timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH review and award timelines can be prolonged (examples: submission → SRG review → summary statement → council review → pending admin review → JIT → award prepared → NOA), sometimes delayed by pandemics, continuing resolutions, or internal IC practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain patience, keep the PO informed, and plan backups (resubmissions, alternative funding). Sharing timelines (as forum members did) helps set expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Score release timing and possible post-meeting corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Scores are generally finalized at the meeting but may not be released immediately; SROs may wait up to three business days to check for mistakes or outliers and reviewers sometimes request corrections afterward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect possible delays in score release and in email notification; minor changes/corrections can occur and SROs may intentionally delay release to verify scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: FOA- and mechanism-specific eligibility and timing considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Different FOAs and mechanisms (e.g., DP2, K99, R25, PARs) have distinct eligibility rules, numbers of awards, and award timing (e.g., some awards are all issued at a single time of year or require tenure-track activation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check FOA details and ask PO about timing and eligibility nuances (e.g., whether DP2 awards require being faculty to activate, how many awards an IC typically makes, whether K99 timelines differ). Consider alternative mechanisms (e.g., R01) if eligibility windows or timing constrain you.

rubrics_metrics.name: New Investigator / ESI status impacts and extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: ESI status can sometimes be extended (e.g., for COVID-related disruptions) via eRA Commons requests; New Investigator recognition and ESI weighting vary by IC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit ESI extension requests through the Education section of eRA Commons if applicable, and consult the PO about whether your NI/ESI status will influence payline or select pay consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPI structure and New Investigator designation
rubrics_metrics.description: Handling of New Investigator status in MPI arrangements can be complex (e.g., contact PI being a New Investigator may not change review outcome if the MPI structure removes NI recognition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss MPI implications with your PO; administrative requests (like Other Support) are a better immediate signal of interest than assumptions about NI treatment under MPI.
